title: Ablative and vocative

objectives.can: Recognise the ablative and its main uses, and the vocative.

explanation.summary: The ablative is the busiest Latin case: it follows many prepositions, it can say how or with what something is done, and it can say when. The vocative is the case of address, used when you speak to someone. Between them they complete the six cases.

sections.heading: The ablative with prepositions
body: Several of the commonest prepositions take the ablative and no other case: *a* or *ab* ('from', 'by'), *e* or *ex* ('out of'), *de* ('down from', 'about'), *cum* ('with'), *sine* ('without') and *pro* ('for', 'on behalf of'). In *dat pro ovibus suis*, 'he gives his life for his sheep', *ovibus* is ablative because *pro* demands it.

The preposition *in* takes the ablative when it means 'in' or 'on', a place where something is: *in consilio*, 'in the counsel'; *in cathedra*, 'in the seat' (Psalm 1:1). With the accusative it means 'into' or 'against'. L1.3.2 teaches the prepositions in full; for now, learn to recognise a noun after one of them as probably ablative.

sections.heading: The ablative without a preposition: means and time
body: The ablative alone often says by what means or with what instrument something is done. In *igne combussi*, 'I burned it with fire' (Deuteronomy 9:21), *igne* is ablative of means and no preposition is needed.

It also says when something happens: *die ac nocte* in Psalm 1:2 is 'by day and by night', that is, at any time in the day or the night. These uses can be translated 'with', 'by' and 'at', but English chooses its word by the sense, and so must you.

sections.heading: The Vulgate's in with the ablative
body: Where classical Latin would use the ablative alone, the Vulgate often adds *in*: *Ego baptizo in aqua*, 'I baptize with water' (John 1:26). The usage follows the Hebrew and Greek the translation renders, where a similar little word is used for the means or instrument. So *in* with the ablative can mean 'with' or 'by'. The context, and the English alongside, shows when.

sections.heading: The endings of the ablative
body: The ablative singular ends in -a (first declension, with a long a that the edition does not mark), -o (second), -e (third; sometimes -i) and -u (fourth). The plural ends in -is (first and second) or -ibus (the rest). Many of these forms are shared with other cases: the first-declension -a is also the nominative, the second-declension -o is also the dative, and the plural -is and -ibus are also the dative plural. The analysis in this library leaves such forms undecided, which is why the exercises here use only forms with a single certain reading, such as *homine* (third declension, -e) or *manu* (fourth).
A form like *die* shows how confusing this can be: it may be ablative, dative or genitive, and only the sentence decides.

sections.heading: The vocative: addressing someone
body: The vocative names the person or thing spoken to: *Domine, si vis*, 'Lord, if you wish' (Matthew 8:2). In nearly every noun it is the same as the nominative. The one regular difference is in the second declension: a masculine in -us has the vocative in -e (*dominus* gives *domine*; *servus* gives *serve*), and a masculine in -ius has the vocative in -i (*filius* gives *fili*, as in *Confide fili*, 'Take heart, son', Matthew 9:2).

*Deus* has no special vocative: the nominative form addresses God. Because the vocative so often looks like another case, the analysis in this library marks *fili* as genitive or vocative and does not decide; the sense (someone is being spoken to) does. In the exercises, the only vocatives that can be asked about with certainty are those in -e such as *domine*.

misunderstandings: The ablative is not always 'by' or 'with'. After *ab* it is 'from', after *in* it is 'in', and after *pro* it is 'for'. The ablative has many senses and the case alone does not decide the English word.
*in* does not always take the ablative. With the accusative it means 'into' or 'against'. The case of the noun shows which.
The Vulgate's *in aqua* ('with water') is not a mistake. It is a regular feature of the Latin of the Bible, which follows the idiom of the original languages.
*domine* is not a different word from *dominus*: it is the same noun in the vocative. An -e at the end of a Latin noun is not always a vocative, since the third-declension ablative also ends in -e.

deeper.heading: One case, three ancestors
body: In the grammarians' account, the Latin ablative merges three older cases: a true ablative ('from'), an instrumental ('with, by') and a locative ('where, when'). That is why its uses seem so unrelated. Some forms of the locative survive on their own, in words such as *domi* ('at home').

paradigms.caption: commonest endings; shared forms are undecided in the analysed texts

paradigms.note: The vocative equals the nominative except in the second declension: -us gives -e (domine), -ius gives -i (fili).
